name: Confabulation
statement: People produce confident false accounts of their own memories and reasons: a clinical symptom after limbic and frontal damage, and a laboratory finding in healthy adults.
meaning: One word covers two claims of very different strength, and this entry keeps them apart. The clinical claim is that certain patients state as memory things that did not happen, without intent to deceive, and act on them. Clinicians divide these into provoked confabulations, which appear when a patient is questioned and cannot retrieve, and spontaneous confabulations, which the patient offers unasked and behaves according to. Both are rated with validated instruments and both are tied to particular lesions. The second claim is about everybody. It says that when a healthy person explains a choice, the explanation is generated after the fact and need not track what actually drove the choice. That claim has three supporting bodies of work: Nisbett and Wilson's 1977 survey of studies where people misreported what influenced them, Gazzaniga's split-brain patients narrating actions their speaking hemisphere had no access to, and the choice blindness paradigm, in which the outcome of a choice is switched and the person is asked why they chose it. Evidence for one claim is not evidence for the other. A Korsakoff patient inventing a hospital visit and a shopper explaining a jam they did not pick share a description, not a mechanism. Choice blindness is kept here rather than under introspection illusion, entry 167, or rationalisation, entry 335, and both of those entries point at this one. False memory, entry 35, covers suggestion-implanted memories in people without lesions, and narrative bias, entry 290, covers what stories do to risk judgements.

origin.who: Richard E. Nisbett and Timothy DeCamp Wilson
origin.note: This is the origin of the claim about ordinary people, not of the term. Confabulation was a clinical word for most of a century before 1977, and no source establishing its first use was read for this entry. An English translation of Korsakoff appeared in Neurology in 1955 and is listed below unread. The word confabulation does not occur in the scanned text of Nisbett and Wilson's paper searched here; they wrote about the accuracy of verbal reports.

evidence: The clinical work rests on lesion series with instruments built for it. Schnider and Ptak gave amnesic patients repeated runs of a continuous recognition task. Spontaneous confabulators detected target items as accurately as nonconfabulating amnesics, and increasingly failed to suppress false positives, confusing an earlier run with the current one. Lesions involved the anterior limbic system: medial orbitofrontal cortex, basal forebrain, amygdala and perirhinal cortex or medial hypothalamus. Schnider, Ptak, von Däniken and Remonda re-examined eight patients 18 months after onset. Seven stopped confabulating, and temporal context confusion tracked the clinical course while standard memory and executive tests did not. Rensen and colleagues built the Nijmegen-Venray Confabulation List so caregivers could rate spontaneous as well as provoked confabulation, validating the 20-item version on 28 Korsakoff patients and 24 cognitively impaired chronic alcoholics against the Dalla Barba Confabulation Battery and the Provoked Confabulation Test. A later factor analysis on 252 patients with alcoholic Korsakoff's syndrome preferred a four-factor structure to the original three. That paper reports no internal consistency of its own. The lambda 2 values it prints, 0.75 for provoked and 0.91 for spontaneous confabulation, are quoted from the 2015 validation on the smaller sample, and they appear here at one remove. The claim about healthy people starts from thinner material. Nisbett and Wilson's stocking study came, in their own word, serendipitously, out of a failed attempt to manipulate the smell of garments. Passersby in commercial premises evaluated four identical pairs of nylon stockings, 52 subjects in that study and 378 in a companion study using four different nightgowns. The right-most stockings were preferred over the left-most by a factor of almost four to one. No subject spontaneously mentioned position, and asked directly, virtually all denied it. That section of the paper carries no percentage, no test statistic and no control condition. Gazzaniga's demonstration is a single patient. Gazzaniga, LeDoux and Wilson reported P.S. in 1977 as a 15-year-old callosally sectioned boy whose mute right hemisphere could comprehend nouns and verbs and spell with the left hand. In the test the retellings use, a chicken claw was shown to P.S.'s speaking left hemisphere and a snow scene to his right. From eight pictures his left hand chose a snow shovel and his right a chicken, and he said the chicken claw goes with the chicken, and you need a shovel to clean out the chicken shed. Johansson, Hall, Sikström and Olsson turned the claim into a repeatable procedure. They ran 120 participants through 15 pairs of female faces, asked which face was more attractive, and used a double-card ploy to hand back the rejected face on three trials. Two participants were dropped for seeing how the trick worked, which leaves 118 in the analysis and 354 manipulated trials, of which 46, or 13%, were caught as they happened. Tallying every form of detection including the post-experiment interview left no more than 26% exposed. Blind raters found no difference between reports for real and switched choices on emotionality, specificity or certainty, and none in length, tense or laughter. They did find more self-questioning commentary in the switched reports, t(118) = 3.31, p < 0.005, though it appeared in 5% of them.

replication.headline: Switch the outcome of a choice and ask why, and every laboratory that has tried it gets accepted and justified reversals, in Sweden, Argentina, the Netherlands, Singapore, Germany and the United States. How much goes undetected is where they disagree, from 87% of trials in the original to 7% in a computerised repeat.
replication.detail: The largest test is independent of the originating laboratory. Rieznik and colleagues manipulated answers to political questions and report 40% of 131 manipulated trials detected in a laboratory experiment of 56 people, and 55% of 4,848 manipulated questions undetected in an online experiment finished by 3,106 of the 4,537 who started. Hall, Johansson and Strandberg reversed two of twelve moral ratings for 160 people. About a third of trials were caught concurrently in one condition and close to half in the other, 69% of participants accepted at least one reversal, and 53% argued unequivocally for the opposite of their original position on at least one trial. Strandberg, Sivén, Hall, Johansson and Pärnamets recruited 150 and analysed 140, found half the manipulations corrected, and found that confabulating supporting arguments produced larger attitude shifts a week later. Their second experiment recruited 264 and analysed 232, and 234 of its 464 manipulated trials, 50.4%, were corrected. Strandberg, Olson, Hall, Woods and Johansson preregistered the design and analysis of a test on American voters at https://osf.io/gzymp. Approaching people at the first 2016 presidential debate and in New York parks, they analysed 122 of 136 and found 12% of manipulations corrected, 95% CI 8% to 17%. An online run on 498 Americans found 41% of 2,025 manipulations corrected. In a supermarket, Hall and colleagues switched jam and tea samples on 180 shoppers and detected 14.4% of manipulated jam trials and 13.8% of tea trials concurrently, 33.3% and 32.2% counting every form. Sauerland, Sagana, Otgaar and Broers took the procedure to 87 adolescents and 117 children and report blindness rates from 37% to 91% concurrently and 27% to 47% in retrospect. Patterson and colleagues put it into a simulated intelligence task and report that 76% of novices missed the switch, then set aside the participants who noticed and ignored it, which leaves a choice-blind group of about 20% to 25% of the sample. Experts behaved like novices. The disagreement is about how much, and about what an undetected trial means. Grassi, Hoeppe, Baytimur and Bartels ran 41 participants through 328 manipulated trials, got 56.4% concurrent reporting against 84.45% on later questioning, and were left with 7% of trials never reported at all. They read the gap as covert detection rather than blindness. Their pupil evidence is thinner than that reading needs: the t-tests are one-sided, and the trials nobody ever reported gave only a numerically larger pupil response, on 11 participants and 16 trials. Marchant and colleagues showed across three experiments that cues suggesting the experimenter was incompetent raised reporting, which points the same way. Taya, Gupta, Farber and Mullette-Gillman found 16.9% concurrent detection across 160 manipulated trials from 32 people in Singapore, rising to 75% of participants once queried afterwards. No multi-laboratory test was located, and no direct repeat of Nisbett and Wilson's stocking study; searches ran across PubMed, Europe PMC, Crossref, PLOS, Frontiers and the open web. None of this touches the clinical syndrome.

study.cite: Rieznik, A., Moscovich, L., Frieiro, A., Figini, J., Catalano, R., Garrido, J. M., Alvarez Heduan, F., Sigman, M., & Gonzalez, P. A. (2017). A massive experiment on choice blindness in political decisions: Confidence, confabulation, and unconscious detection of self-deception. PLoS ONE, 12(2), e0171108.

limits: The verdict above is about the choice blindness procedure and nothing else. The clinical syndrome is not something a replication verdict fits: it is a lesion-linked symptom described in patient series of eight, 28, 172 and 252, not an effect with an original and a repeat. Those series do not agree with each other on course. Schnider and colleagues found seven of eight patients had stopped confabulating by 18 months, while Oudman, Rensen and Kessels rated 172 patients with alcoholic Korsakoff's syndrome and found provoked and spontaneous confabulation present in the chronic phase as well as the post-acute one. The stocking study has its own verdict, which is that the evidence is weak. Fifty-two shoppers, one ratio, no test statistic, no control, and the authors themselves list it among the studies where subjects may have denied the influential stimulus to avoid looking silly or foolish rather than because they were unaware of it. Position effects in later work do not point one way. Bar-Hillel's review, read here only as an abstract, describes them as seemingly inconsistent: first position wins on ballots, middle on multiple-choice tests and supermarket shelves, first or last on restaurant menus. Christenfeld's 1995 study of choices from identical options is the nearest thing located to a repeat of the stocking design and could not be obtained. Unpaywall records no open copy, Europe PMC has no record of it, the Semantic Scholar link to the author's university page returns 404 and the publisher returns 403, so nothing from it is used here. The split-brain evidence is a demonstration, not a measurement. The quoted exchange with P.S. is reproduced in a review Gazzaniga co-wrote, which attributes it to his own 2000 paper; that paper could not be reached at the publisher, and the wording used here was taken twice from the review's own figure caption. De Haan and eleven colleagues note that split-brain findings come from a relatively small group of patients who differ among themselves, some with all commissures severed and some with only the corpus callosum cut. Pinto and seven colleagues tested two patients with radiologically confirmed complete transection and found awareness of stimulus presence across the whole visual field whichever hand or voice answered, which they read as divided perception without divided consciousness. Johansson and colleagues' 2005 Science paper and their 2006 follow-up were read in full from author-posted copies of the published versions, as were Hall and colleagues' 2010 supermarket study and Strandberg and colleagues' 2018 paper. The percentages in the 2005 figure of eight report categories, which include a specific confabulation category and an original choice category, sit in an image and were not read. The clinical papers were read as abstracts except the 2021 factor analysis, which was read at PubMed Central. Kopelman's review, Dalla Barba's battery and Bar-Hillel's review are named from their abstracts, and Patterson and colleagues' military study is paywalled at the publisher and was read as a structured abstract. Korsakoff's 1955 translation is listed because it exists. Unpaywall records no open copy and Europe PMC holds no abstract, and it was not read.
misreadings: The stocking study is retold with numbers it does not contain. Popular versions give a percentage choosing the right-hand pair and describe every participant offering a detailed account of texture and weave. The paper reports a four-to-one ratio between the ends of the array and says only that no subject mentioned position and that virtually all denied it when asked. The knit, sheerness and weave appear in the authors' theorising about which causes feel plausible, not in a record of what shoppers said. The word confabulation does not occur in the scan of that paper searched here. The 13% figure from Johansson and colleagues is quoted as the detection rate. It is the concurrent rate; their own all-forms figure is 26%, and later designs run far higher, to 92.1% of manipulated trials reported in one computerised study. Headline rates are quoted without the authors' own adjustments. Patterson and colleagues' 76% is the proportion who failed to detect the switch, and the same paper puts the choice-blind group at about a fifth to a quarter of the sample once participants who noticed and ignored the switch are set aside. Clinical and everyday confabulation are treated as one thing on the strength of the shared word. Provoked and spontaneous confabulation come apart even inside Korsakoff's syndrome: Rensen and colleagues found provoked confabulation associated with executive dysfunction and poorer memory, and spontaneous confabulation associated with neither. Choice blindness is read as showing that stated reasons are always invented. Johansson and colleagues' own coding kept a category for reports that must have been about the original choice, because they contradicted the face the participant was holding. The split-brain interpreter is offered as a general fact about left hemispheres. It rests on demonstrations in a handful of patients who had epilepsy severe enough to warrant surgery and who differ in how much was cut.
